# Your tasks:

+ Use the data set "/Data/GradSchool_Admissions.csv"
+ You will explore and model the predictors of graduate school admission
  - the "admit" column is coded as 1=success and 0=failure (that's binary, so model appropriately)
  - the other columns are the GRE score, the GPA, and the rank of the undergraduate institution, where I is "top-tier."
+ Document your data explorations, figures, and conclusions in a reproducible R-markdown report
+ That means I want to see, in your html report, your process of model evaluation and selection. Here's an [example](https://gzahn.github.io/data-course/Repository/Assignments/Assignment_9/example.html){target="_blank"}
+ Upload your **self-contained** R project, including knitted HTML report, to GitHub in *your* Assignment_9 directory


# First I had to load in the required packages #

library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(readxl)

# Then I had to load in the data set that I would be using and analyzing #

grad <- read_csv("GradSchool_Admissions.csv")

# Then I had to clean up some of the data to make it more usable in R studio #
# The first thing I did was convert the rank column into a categorical factor with 1 as the baseline #

grad_clean <- grad %>%
  mutate(
    admit_factor = factor(admit, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    rank = factor(rank)
  )

# Then I wanted to see what that now looked like using this code #

glimpse(grad_clean)

# Then I wanted to check for missing values in each column #

colSums(is.na(grad_clean))

# Then I continued using the clean data and summarized count, admission rate, mean gre, and mean gpa for each rank level #

grad_clean %>%
  group_by(rank) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    admit_rate = mean(admit),
    mean_gre = mean(gre),
    mean_gpa = mean(gpa),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Then I needed to change the data from wide format to long format #

grad_long <- grad_clean %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(gre, gpa), names_to = "metric", values_to = "score")
  
# Then it was time to start plotting #
# I decided to make box plots #
# The first plot compares the test scores and the GPA of students who had been admitted and those that had not #
# This first graph shows that the students who did get admitted often have higher GRE scoes and GPAs. #

ggplot(grad_long, aes(x = admit_factor, y = score, fill = admit_factor)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.75, outlier.alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")


# This next plot shows the admission percentage for each school rank # 
# This plot demonstrates that the admission rates of undergradautes from a rank 1 school is much hiugher than a student from a rank 4 school #

ggplot(grad_clean, aes(x = rank, fill = admit_factor)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  theme_minimal()
  
# After that it was time to generate a model for the data set #
# I decided to just do one model that investigates the importance of each variable rather than making a different model for each factor # 
# That code looked like this #
  
logit_model <- glm(admit ~ gre + gpa + rank, data = grad_clean, family = binomial)

# this summary command shows the generated raw log-odds output #
# The tidy command gives the odds ratios # 

summary(logit_model)
tidy(logit_model, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
  
# These scripts demonstrate the importance of each of the factors #
# In the tidy data the code looks at each factor individually and generates a ratio of how much each factor helps or hurts your odds of admission #
# After running the data it is is clear that increasing yoru GRE scores and your GPA have a strong connection to increasing your odds of being admitted #
# It also demonstrates that coming from a rank 1 school is much better than a rank 2 and even coming from a rank four school decreases your chances of being admitted all the way down to 20 % #
# These are very interesting numbers in terms of how to get the best chance of making it into your desired school #
# It also gives insight into how to imporve your chances of being admitted #

# Next I wanted to look at each applicant in the data and give them a predicted probability of admission using this given model # 
# That was done using the code below #

grad_pred <- grad_clean %>%
  mutate(pred_prob = predict(logit_model, type = "response"))

# You can then look at that data using the following code #

head(grad_pred)

# Next I wanted to generate a plot with a predicted probability curve for each rank #
# First I had to create a table of every possible combination of the values in the original data #
# The mutate portion takes each of the 400 hypothetical students created in the expand_grid and calculates the predicted admission probability for each so they can then be plotted on the ggplot after that #
# That code looks like the following #

pred_grid <- expand_grid(
  gpa = seq(min(grad_clean$gpa), max(grad_clean$gpa), length.out = 100),
  gre = mean(grad_clean$gre),
  rank = factor(1:4, levels = levels(grad_clean$rank))
) %>%
  mutate(pred_prob = predict(logit_model, newdata = ., type = "response"))

# After building that grid it is now time to plot it on a predicted probability curve # 
# That code goes as follows #

ggplot(pred_grid, aes(x = gpa, y = pred_prob, color = rank)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "GPA",
    y = "Predicted Probability of Admission",
    color = "School Rank"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


# After cleaning the data, running it through ggplot for exploratory data analysis it is clear that all three of the factors generated play a statistically significant role in the probability of a student to get admitted or not #
# The data clearly shows that the higher your GRE scores the more likely you are to be admitted. #
# It shows that the higher your GPA is the more likely you are to be admitted # 
# And it demonstrates that what rank fo undergraduate school you come from also plays a significant role. #
# The final data graph visibly demonstrates the role each factor plays and what it means for the slope of your predicted probablity of admission. #
